title: Time-delayed feedback turns Arrhenius escape logarithmic
authors: Roy Podgaetsky, Vishwajeet Kumar Arnab Pal, Ohad Shpielberg
abstract: Thermal escape is governed by the Arrhenius law, where the mean escape time scales exponentially with the barrier height. We show that the non-Markovianity induced by time-delayed feedback in the confining force removes this exponential scaling. Beyond a threshold set by the curvature of the minimum, the delay destabilizes the well, and the thermal noise seeds an instability that is subsequently amplified deterministically to the boundary leading to \textit{slingshot} escape trajectories. The escape time becomes logarithmic in the barrier, its fluctuations follow a Gumbel law, and an optimal delay enables escape faster than free diffusion. Our results propose time delay as a tunable and experimentally feasible control parameter for accelerating activated processes.
summary: This theoretical work analyzes how time-delayed feedback fundamentally alters thermal escape dynamics, replacing the standard exponential Arrhenius law with a logarithmic dependence on the barrier height. By inducing a deterministic 'slingshot' instability, the delay acts as a tunable control parameter, enabling escape significantly faster than predicted by classical theories.
main_problem: The paper investigates how time-delayed feedback modifies the standard Arrhenius exponential scaling governing thermally activated escape over an energy barrier.
main_result: The mean escape time transitions from exponential to a logarithmic dependence on the barrier height, $\langle T angle \propto \ln(\Delta U/D)$, due to a deterministic 'slingshot' escape mechanism.
method: The analysis involves solving the non-Markovian Langevin equation, identifying a Hopf bifurcation point, and deriving the escape time by analyzing the two-stage process of noise-seeded diffusion followed by deterministic amplification.
model_or_system: The system is an overdamped particle diffusing in a confining potential $U(x)$, subjected to a time-delayed conservative force: $\gamma \dot{x}(t) = -U'(x(t-	au)) + \sqrt{2D} \eta(t)$.
key_observables: Mean escape time $\langle T angle$, which exhibits a Gumbel distribution for its fluctuations.
important_parameters: Dimensionless delay $s = 	au/	au_{	ext{relax}}$, barrier-to-noise ratio $\Delta U/D$, and the critical delay $s_c = \pi/2$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the system is overdamped and the delay only affects the conservative force; the logarithmic law is derived for the weak-noise regime ($\Delta U/D \gg 1$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the contrast between Arrhenius and Slingshot escape trajectories, confirm the universal logarithmic slope $A(s)$ across different potentials, and show the Gumbel distribution of the escape-time histogram.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the non-Markovian dynamics, identifies the instability threshold ($s_c$), derives the logarithmic escape law $\langle T angle \propto \ln(\Delta U/D)$ by analyzing the envelope crossing, and discusses the implications for tunable control of activated processes.
why_interesting: The replacement of exponential scaling with a logarithmic dependence is a profound non-equilibrium effect, providing a new, controllable mechanism for accelerating processes relevant to quantum tunneling or barrier crossing in open quantum systems.

Each falls sharply past sc = π/2 to a minimum near s ≃3 — exponentially faster than Arrhenius, and below the free-diffusion time — then saturates to the diffusive limit in large s. The non-monotonic shape is a generic feature of slingshot escape. Middle: Universality of the logarithmic slope.
